case.label: A
case.text: Spread placement puts each instance on separate hardware and also supports six instances in one zone, so it could be argued as the safe choice; but it gives no low-latency or high-throughput networking, which the stem asks for.

case.label: A
case.text: Moving the primary interface looks like the most direct way to carry addresses and MAC to the standby, but the primary network interface (eth0) cannot be detached from an instance, so it fails.

case.label: D
case.text: Storage optimized instances have large memory and fast local storage, so they could hold a data set, but the stem shows memory pressure with low disk activity, so memory optimized fits and storage does not.

case.label: A
case.text: Frequent key rotation might be called a security improvement, but it keeps SSH keys, the bastion and open inbound port 22, which the stem forbids.

case.label: A
case.text: Launching a new instance from an AMI leaves the old one running until clients move, which can mean less downtime than a stop and start; but it loses data written after the AMI, changes addresses and runs two copies, which the application cannot do.

case.label: C
case.text: Partition placement groups isolate partitions from each other's hardware, which could be read as meeting the requirement; but three instances share a partition, so one hardware failure can affect three of them.

case.label: C
case.text: Lambda container images are serverless and cheap and run on a schedule, so a candidate might choose it; but a Lambda invocation is limited to 15 minutes, and the job runs 40 to 90 minutes.

case.label: D
case.text: A runbook costs nothing until a disaster and needs no copies; but installing and configuring by hand is slow and error-prone, so identical instances within 1 hour is not assured and it is not low overhead.

answers.flag: Option B (enable hibernation on running instances) is defensible if the current EC2 service allows enabling hibernation on an existing instance, which the stem does not settle; the facts of the chapter must show that hibernation can only be set at launch.

case.label: B
case.text: Enabling hibernation on the existing instances and calling the stop API with the hibernate parameter needs no replacement of instances, so it would be the lowest overhead if EC2 allowed hibernation to be turned on after launch.

case.label: A
case.text: A higher maximum price sounds like it would reduce interruptions, but Spot interruptions are driven by capacity, and the price is no longer what drives them, so it does not meet the requirement.

case.label: A
case.text: A stop and start moves the instance to a new host and keeps the instance ID, private IP and Elastic IP, so a Lambda function would also meet the need; but it is custom code to build and run, so it has more overhead than the built-in recover action.

case.label: B
case.text: A 3-year All Upfront Reserved Instance has the lowest hourly rate, so a candidate might call it cheapest; but it bills every hour for 3 years while the job uses 3 hours a day, so On-Demand costs less.

case.label: D
case.text: Two active Regions would survive an AZ failure and so look like extra safety; but the stem asks only for AZ failure tolerance, so the second Region only adds cost.

case.label: C
case.text: Dedicated Instances give single-tenant hardware and might look cheaper than hosts; but they give no visibility into sockets and physical cores, so they cannot satisfy the reporting duty and per-core licence terms.

case.label: D
case.text: Standard mode ends surplus credit charges and so lowers the bill; but at 80% CPU against a lower baseline the instance would be throttled, which breaks the performance requirement.

case.label: B
case.text: On-Demand has no interruption risk and is simple; but with a job that tolerates interruption, Spot gives the same result at a lower price.

case.label: D
case.text: Keeping three zones with more nodes keeps the cluster highly available, but it does nothing to the cross-zone transfer charges, and the stem says high availability is not needed.

answers.flag: The stem gives no instance size or Savings Plan combination, so a Dedicated Host (A) could also guarantee capacity and may cost less than On-Demand pricing for a full-time Capacity Reservation; and a Savings Plan paired with the reservation would beat the reservation alone.

case.label: A
case.text: Allocating Dedicated Hosts in the zone also holds capacity for all 8 instances, and for large instances a host could cost no more than 8 On-Demand instances, with host reservations giving a discount, so it could be called both a capacity and a cost answer.

case.label: D
case.text: Running through the night avoids the load with no change, and a Savings Plan reduces the price; but paying for idle hours is still more than hibernating, so it is not the most cost-effective.

case.label: D
case.text: A smaller general purpose instance sized for the 9% average is the cheapest on paper; but the 85% peaks would then exceed its CPU, so mornings would be slow.

case.label: D
case.text: Changing the instance type is the smallest step, and Python does not depend on the CPU; but an x86 AMI cannot boot on an arm64 Graviton type, and the C helper must be recompiled.

case.label: C
case.text: A Compute Savings Plan covers the same usage with more flexibility, and a careful candidate may prefer it; but the stem fixes the family and Region for 3 years, so flexibility is not needed and the EC2 Instance Savings Plan gives the larger discount.
